messages.subject: Re: Questions about CODEX
messages.body_plain:
Dear Yuchao,

I'm sorry to bother you again but I have another question regarding CODEX.
In your analysis, do you pre-process the BAM file before performing normalization and CNV Calling?
I'm asking this because right now I'm using mainly .bam files preprocessed using the standard workflow for variant calling in exome data (so marking duplicates, realign reads around known indels, recalibrate the QC and so on). In your experience does this affect variant calling and what pre-processing would you recommend, if any?

Again, thanks for your availability and your kindness,

Best,

Daniele

> > I'm Daniele Capocefalo, a computational biologist that is approaching the CNV discovery in WES experiments. I'm trying to use your algorithm o test for CNVs in my experiments. I followed the guidelines described in your Bioconductor vignettes. However, I have a couple of questions on regard:
> > I've noticed that in your tutorial you can search for CNV one chromosome at a time. Nevertheless, would it be possible to search for CNV in a genome wide fashion? Or I have to repeat the procedure for each chromosome (maybe looping for it)?
> >
> > Yes, CODEX processes each chromosome separately due to two reasons: (i) to save computation time for the normalization algorithm, which depends on the number of exons; (ii) the segmentation is performed within each chromosome separately. This applies to almost all CNV calling algorithm that we are aware of. Yes, you need to loop for it or use parallel computing on HPC (recommended).
> > According to your guidelines, in the final file (CODEX_frac.txt) there should be a last lines representing the p-value computed using the Wilk's test. However, both in your tutorial and in some tests I ran i haven't found the pvalue column. Should I specify it somewhere?
> >
> > We decided to remove the p-values since they are all towards the very extreme end near 0 and we are not sure how the p-value behaves in this extreme case. With this said, if you use the integer mode for segmentation, all CNVs reported are significant by CODEX; if you use the fractional mode for segmentation (for cancer samples for example), you need to have a threshold on the segmented copy numbers. Under both scenarios, it is recommended that you load your calling results across all samples into IGV for visualization (how to do this is in our GitHub page).
> > From your tutorial, I understood that it is possible to use a control sample with no CNVs in order test the other samples against the former one. How many control samples would you recommend to use? The "normal_index" parameters specify the index of the normal samples in the bamdir object?
> >
> > Yes, the normal_index specifies the index of the normal samples in the order you feed them to CODEX. If you are calling germline CNVs, this doesn’t make too much difference. However if you are calling samples from a mixture of tumor-normal pairs, this makes a difference since the tumor samples share significant recurrent changes which can be treated as an artifact by CODEX. With this said, the more normal samples you have (from the same batch!), the better. So that CODEX can capture the biases and artifacts from the batch using the normal samples while maintaining the CNV signals in the tumor samples.
> > Using the "normalize" function, you use 9 latent poisson factors. How was the choice behind this and would you recommend to use another number of latent factors in other settings/conditions?
> >
> > From our experiences, K=1:10 is usually enough. To choose an optimal K is non-trivial, you can refer to the AIC, BIC, RSS plot generated by CODEX. Sometimes we also look at regions where known CNVs are expected as a sanity check.
> > How should I interpret the "mBIC" column? Larger score means higher likelihood of the CNV to be present?
> >
> > It’s the modified BIC that offers a guidance in the segmentation step. It tells the segmentation when to stop. BIC = 2 ln(L) − k ln(n) where the first part is the log likelihood and the second part is penalty on model complexity.
> >
> > Thanks a lot for your time and patience and apologise if the questions sounds too trivial, I have just started getting into this field!

messages.subject: Re: Questions about CODEX
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniele,

The pre-processing of bams for GATK/MuTect calling should not have too much effect on CNV calling. There is a step in CODEX where the reads with low mapping qualities and the duplicated reads are removed. The pre-processing procedure makes this step more accurate. Although we haven’t done any testings, we believe the pre-processing have small effect on large CNV detection.

Hope that this clarifies,
Yuchao

messages.body_plain:
Hi-

I am trying to use CODEX with the following code, but have encountered two error messages.
As you can see from the first error message, I tried to use Rsamtools to read in my bam, and
then converted the list to a dataframe. But then I ran into a second error message (bottom).
Can anyone help me troubleshoot these error messages?

CODEX - Steps
#############################################
code chunk number 3: bambedObj1
#############################################

Library(Rsamtools)
Library(CODEX)

setwd("/Data/CODEX/tumor")
dirPath_tumor <- ("/Data/CODEX/tumor")
bamFile_tumor <- list.files(dirPath_tumor, pattern='*.bam$')
bamdir_tumor <- file.path(dirPath_tumor, bamFile_tumor)

sampname <- as.matrix(read.table(file.path(dirPath_tumor, "sample.bam")))
Error in scan(file = file, what = what, sep = sep, quote = quote, dec = dec,  :
  line 1 did not have 3 elements
In addition: Warning message:
In read.table(file.path(dirPath_tumor, "sample.bam")) :
  line 1 appears to contain embedded nulls

WORK AROUND
library(Rsamtools)
bam <- scanBam("sample.bam")  // replaces the code sampname <- as.matrix(read.table(file.path(dirPath, "sampname"))) //
bam_tumor <- as.data.frame(bam)

sampname <- bam_tumor
bedFile_tumor <- file.path(dirPath_tumor, "sample.bed")
chr <- 1
bambedObj_tumor <- getbambed(bamdir = bamdir_tumor, bedFile=bedFile_tumor, sampname=bam_tumor, projectname="project", chr)
bamdir <- bambedObj_tumor$bamdir_tumor
sampname <- bambedObj_tumor$sampname
ref <- bambedObj_tumor$ref
projectname <- bambedObj_tumor$projectname
chr <- bambedObj_tumor$chr

#####################################
code chunk number 4:coverageObj1
#####################################

coverageObj <- getcoverage(bambedObj_tumor, mapqthres = 30)

Getting coverage for sample K00171:238:H7JKLBBXX:6:2210:19451:33088: read length 100.
Error in BamFile(file, index) : 'file' must be character(1) and not NA

Many Thanks,
Margaret

messages.subject: Re: Question about CODEX analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Noemie,

Thanks and no problem! We welcome all questions! We use that to cap the copy numbers but if you like you can of course remove that line and source the function after loading CODEX. The reason that we remove that is because sometimes we want to visualize the copy numbers returned by CODEX and very large copy numbers distorts the range of the plot, for example. Also, in cancer genomics, we categorize any copy number alteration event with copy number >=4 as high gain so all the events will be counted as high gain as compared to gain.

Hope that this clarifies!
Yuchao

> On Nov 17, 2016, at 5:47 AM, Noemie Leblay <leb...@students.iarc.fr> wrote:
>

> Hi Yuchao,
>
> I hope this email finds you well.
>
> Sorry we have another question for you.
> We checked your script in the segment function and we saw “chat[chat > 5] <- 5” (line 38). Why do you limit the duplication copy number to 5? Do you have a methodologic/ biological reason? (we know that the other CNV analysis methods can give larger copy number estimates).

>
> Thank you so much in advance.
>
> Best regards
>
>

> Noémie & Nicolas

>
>
> From: Jiang, Yuchao [mailto:yuc...@wharton.upenn.edu]
> Sent: Saturday, October 15, 2016 6:10 PM
> To: Noemie Leblay
> Cc: Lynnette Fernandez Cuesta; Nicolas Alcala; codex_...@googlegroups.com
> Subject: RE: Question about CODEX analysis
>
> Hi Noemie,
>
> To determine the number of latent factors is an active research area in statistics and is non-trivial. We included AIC, BIC, and RSS in CODEX to help the users make the optimal choice. However, sometimes as you said, none of these three metrics give an clear solution. From our experiences we also see sometimes they are monotonic and sometimes there is a sudden valley or peak due to the algorithm not converging. You should definitely not choose a optK at values where the algorithm doesn’t converge, for example, K=6 and 7 from chr7. For your dataset, I would probably go with optK=2 and since all chromosomes from the genome/exome are processed in the same batch, ideally this optimal choice should be the same for all chromosomes. We separate the analysis by chromosome to speed up computation, to help the algorithm converge, and to perform segmentation within each chromosome. With this said, we always load our final segmentation results from CODEX to a genome viewer, IGV for example, and look for regions where we know there are germline/somatic CNVs expected. You may want to try different optK values and see if the signals are these places are successfully recovered.
>
> Finally, since you have normal tumor samples and you use the normalize2 function with the normal index as an argument, the exon-wise latent factor is essentially only estimated using the normal samples. Therefore, the choice of optK doesn’t have too much effect on the calling of somatic CNV events. This is what we see from our experience too.
>
> Hope that this clarifies!
>
> Cheers,
> Yuchao
>
>
>
>
> From: Noemie Leblay [mailto:leb...@students.iarc.fr]
> Sent: Friday, October 14, 2016 12:00 PM
> To: Jiang, Yuchao <yuc...@wharton.upenn.edu>
> Cc: Lynnette Fernandez Cuesta <Fernande...@iarc.fr>; Nicolas Alcala <Alc...@fellows.iarc.fr>
> Subject: RE: Question about CODEX analysis
>
> Hi Yuchao,
>
> I hope this email find you well.
> Sorry I have some others questions for you.
>
> I (together with my supervisor Lynnette and coworker Nicolas; CC) ran 55 cases-controls (110 samples total) using recommended parameters for qc function, and the normalize2 function with a number of latent Poisson factors between 1 and 10. I obtained some RSS, AIC, and BIC pdf files that are similar to your example (see chr1), that is, a monotonically decreasing RSS as a function of K, a BIC with an elbow where the optimal K is obvious.
>
> Nevertheless, I also obtain weird RSS, AIC, and BIC values. I have two types of weird results. First, ones where the AIC and BIC increase monotonically over the specified range of K, or plateau after a threshold value of K (see Chr3). I guess these correspond to cases where the K value maximizing the AIC is >10, but I am not sure if it is a good idea to increase K too much, especially when the slope of the BIC is small. Second, ones where the AIC and BIC present “dips” (see Chr6 and 7). I guess these are cases where the maximum likelihood algorithm did not converge properly for some K values. I tried tuning the threshold values for beta hat and h hat in the normalize2 function to force a better convergence; it did reduce the size of the dips, but they are still there.
>
> Did you ever see something of the sort in your previous tests? Do you have recommendations regarding the way to find the optimal K when BIC do not provide a clear answer? How much does the value of K influence the results in such cases and how can we be sure to obtain conservative results?
>
> Thank you so much in advance.
>
> Best regards
>
>
> Noémie

messages.subject: RE: CODEX: optimal K
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. From our daily practice, we never run CODEX with K greater than 15. The glm iterative estimation procedure would be very unstable once the number of latent factors reach above 10. We’ve adopted optK=6 for 300 tumor samples. One thing you have to bear in mind is that, CODEX is only suitable to call rare somatic CNVs using tumor samples only (e.g., the ATRX nested deletion example in our paper). For common somatic CNV detection, you will have to include normal samples and use normalize2() function with an argument of the indices of the normal samples. This step is crucial otherwise your common CNV signals will be removed by latent factors.

Please let me know if you have further questions. I am cc’ing our mailing list in case other people have similar questions.

Cheers,

Yuchao

messages.subject: RE: CODEX: optimal K
messages.body_plain:
Again I would strongly recommend including normal samples in your analysis otherwise your CNV signals, especially the common ones, will be dampened by the normalization procedure. So I would suggest resign your analysis 2. To determine the optimal number of latent factors is not trivial. CODEX outputs a pdf plot by default with results by RSS, AIC and BIC and uses BIC as the default metric. Sometimes the optimal choice of K is unclear. In this case, it would help to visualize the normalization/segmentation results and zoom into regions where you expect known/previously reported CNVs. You can load CODEX’s results into IGV for visualization. There is a script on our GitHub page that generates input for IGV.

Cheers,

Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: CODEX problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Merzu,

Thanks very much for your interest in CODEX! While we said in our GitHub page that CODEX can be applied to the mouse genome, we currently don’t have the bandwidth to maintain or update that part of CODEX. With this said, for the human genome, we calculated the mappability in advance and pre-stored the results in CODEX’s R package and for you error, I feel one of your targets in your bed file might not be sorted, i.e., the start position is larger than the end position. To bypass the error that you encountered, you can: (1) set mappability for all targets/exons to 1 when you run CODEX (essentially mappability is only used in QC to filter out targets and by setting all to 1 you don’t filter out any targets due to low mappability) (2) get mappability from previous annotations, e.g., UCSC.

Let me know if you have further questions.

Best,
Yuchao
